extracted.intended_audience: media scholars, journalism students, researchers of news production, and newsroom practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Apply the Shoemaker & Reese Hierarchy of Influences model to explain or evaluate why particular news stories are selected and how content is shaped across multiple interacting levels from individual journalists to society-wide systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual Level
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal characteristics, beliefs, values, and roles of journalists
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes demographic background, education, religion, political leanings, professional values internalized through socialization, and personal ethics. These individual traits shape reporters' judgments about what is newsworthy and how stories are framed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media Routines Level
rubrics_metrics.description: Practices and norms developed to manage workload; news values themselves are routines (Galtung-Ruge factors)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encompasses beat structures, reliance on official sources, use of the inverted pyramid structure, deadlines and news cycles, and source–reporter relationships. Routine practices prioritize certain types of events and sources, making some topics more likely to be covered and shaping story form and content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational Level
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal newsroom structure, ownership, business model, and editorial policy of the outlet
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covers the position of the journalist within the organizational hierarchy, newsroom culture and routines, and resource allocation. Editorial agendas, management priorities, and economic constraints influence which stories are assigned, how much reporting resources are devoted, and what angles are pursued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social Institutional Level (extramedia)
rubrics_metrics.description: External institutions and forces interacting with the newsroom
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes government, advertisers, audiences, interest groups, public relations actors, and other external sources; also market pressures and the legal/regulatory environment. These extramedia actors exert source pressure, shape access, and create incentives or disincentives for covering certain issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social System Level
rubrics_metrics.description: Broad societal forces shaping media content
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encompasses ideology, culture, the political/economic system, society-wide power structures, and national media system traits. These macro-level conditions define what counts as a problem, set the range of acceptable discourse, and influence long-term norms in news production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implications for Newsworthiness / Story Selection
rubrics_metrics.description: A given story's selection cannot be explained by news values alone; selection is jointly determined by multiple levels
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Story selection results from the interaction of: (1) the reporter's individual judgment (Level 1); (2) routinized news values like timeliness, proximity, and conflict (Level 2); (3) editorial agenda and resource constraints (Level 3); (4) source pressure, market demand, and official statements (Level 4); and (5) ideology and culture that define what counts as a problem (Level 5). Use this multi-level lens when evaluating why particular items appear (or do not appear) on news homepages.
